paragraphs.en: People often complain that plastics are too durable. Water bottles, shopping bags, and other trash litter the planet, from Mount Everest to the Mariana Trench, because plastics are everywhere and don’t break down easily. But some plastic materials change over time. They crack and frizzle. They “weep” out additives. They melt into sludge. All of which creates huge headaches for institutions, such as museums, trying to preserve culturally important objects. The variety of plastic objects at risk is dizzying: early radios, avant-gardesculptures, celluloid animation stills from Disney films, the first artificial heart.
paragraphs.zh: 人们常常抱怨塑料太耐用。从珠穆朗玛峰到马里亚纳海沟，水瓶、购物袋以及其他垃圾散落在地球各处，因为塑料无处不在，而且不易分解。但有些塑料材料会随时间发生变化。它们会开裂、卷缩，会“渗出”添加剂，还会熔化成黏糊状。这一切都让博物馆等试图保存具有重要文化意义物品的机构头痛不已。面临风险的塑料物品种类繁多，令人眼花缭乱：早期收音机、先锋派雕塑、迪士尼电影的赛璐珞动画画稿，以及第一颗人工心脏。

paragraphs.en: Certain artifacts are especially vulnerable because some pioneers in plastic art didn’t always know how to mix ingredients properly, says Thea van Oosten, a polymer chemist who, until retiring a few years ago, worked for decades at the Cultural Heritage Agency of the Netherlands (RCE). “It’s like baking a cake: If you don’t have exact amounts, it goes wrong,” she says. “The object you make isalready a time bomb.”
paragraphs.zh: 聚合物化学家西娅·范奥斯滕表示，有些艺术品尤其脆弱，因为某些塑料艺术先驱并不总是知道如何正确配比原料。她在几年前退休之前，曾在荷兰文化遗产局（RCE）工作了数十年。她说：“这就像烤蛋糕：如果各种原料的用量不准确，就会出问题。你做出来的东西已经是一颗定时炸弹。”

paragraphs.en: And sometimes, it’s not the artist’s fault. In the 1960s, the Italian artist Piero Gilardi began to create hundreds of bright, colorful foam pieces. Thosepieces included small beds of roses and other items as well as a few dozen “ nature carpets ”—large rectangles decorated with foam pumpkins, cabbages, and watermelons. He wanted viewers to walk around on the carpets—whichmeant they had to be durable.
paragraphs.zh: 而有时，这并不是艺术家的错。20世纪60年代，意大利艺术家皮耶罗·吉拉尔迪开始制作数百件色彩鲜艳的泡沫作品。这些作品包括小片玫瑰花坛和其他物品，以及几十件“自然地毯”——在大型长方形地毯上装饰着泡沫制成的南瓜、卷心菜和西瓜。他希望观众能够在地毯上四处走动，这意味着它们必须经久耐用。

paragraphs.en: Unfortunately, the polyurethane foam he used is inherently unstable. It’s especially vulnerable to light damage, and by the mid-1990s, Gilardi’s pumpkins, roses, and other figures were splitting and crumbling. Museums locked some of them away in the dark.
paragraphs.zh: 不幸的是，他所使用的聚氨酯泡沫本身就不稳定。这种材料尤其容易受到光照损伤；到了20世纪90年代中期，吉拉尔迪的南瓜、玫瑰和其他造型开始开裂、碎化。博物馆将其中一些作品收了起来，存放在暗处。

paragraphs.en: So van Oosten and colleagues worked to preserve Gilardi’s sculptures. They infused some with stabilizing and consolidating chemicals. Van Oosten callsthose chemicals “ sunscreens ” because their goal was to prevent further lightdamage and rebuild worn polymer fibers. She is proud that several sculptures have even gone on display again, albeit sometimes beneath protective cases.
paragraphs.zh: 因此，范奥斯滕和同事们开始着手保护吉拉尔迪的雕塑。他们向部分雕塑中注入了起稳定和加固作用的化学物质。范奥斯滕把这些化学物质称为“防晒霜”，因为它们的作用是防止进一步的光照损伤，并修复已经受损的聚合物纤维。令她自豪的是，一些雕塑甚至已重新展出，尽管有时仍罩在保护罩之下。

paragraphs.en: Despite success stories like van Oosten’s, preservation of plastics will likelyget harder. Old objects continue to deteriorate. Worse, biodegradable plastics,designed to disintegrate, are increasingly common.
paragraphs.zh: 尽管有范奥斯滕这样的成功案例，塑料制品的保存今后可能仍会更加困难。老旧物品持续劣化。更糟的是，原本就被设计为能够分解的可生物降解塑料正变得越来越普遍。

paragraphs.en: And more is at stake here than individual objects. Joana Lia Ferreira, anassistant professor of conservation and restoration at the NOVA School of Science and Technology, notes that archaeologists first defined the great material ages of human history—Stone Age, Iron Age, and so on—after examining artifacts inmuseums. We now live in an age of plastic, she says, “and what we decide tocollect today, what we decide to preserve...will have a strong impact on how inthe future we’ll be seen.”
paragraphs.zh: 而这里关系到的远不止一件件物品。里斯本新大学科学与技术学院文物保护与修复助理教授若阿娜·利娅·费雷拉指出，考古学家最初正是在考察了博物馆中的器物后，才划分出人类历史上以材料命名的各个大时代——石器时代、铁器时代，等等。她说，如今我们生活在塑料时代，“而我们今天决定收藏什么、决定保存什么……将会极大地影响未来的人们如何看待我们。”
